text: I have walked the streets of this country as a man and as a question, and I have learned that the two are not so easily separated, that a nation can look at you and decide, before you have spoken, before you have drawn the breath that might have made you human in its eyes, exactly what you are and exactly what you must remain. And I tell you that this looking, this terrible and constant looking, is not the same as being seen. To be seen is to be granted a self; to be looked at in the way I mean is to be told that you have no self to grant, that you are a mirror in which the country studies its own innocence and finds it, always finds it, because it cannot afford to find anything else. I have watched men who would call themselves decent turn away from the simplest truth as though it were a flame, and I have understood that their turning away was not ignorance but labor, the exhausting daily labor of a people who would rather build a myth than look in a glass. We are all of us paying for that labor. We have been paying for it for centuries, and the bill, my friends, has not yet come due in full.

Love is not, whatever the songs may promise, a soft thing; it is the hardest discipline I know, harder than rage, harder than grief, harder even than the patience that injustice demands of those it grinds. To love this country, and I do love it, I love it the way one loves the difficult and the wounding, is to refuse it the comfort of its lies, to stand in the middle of its self-congratulation and say no, no, it did not happen the way you have told it, the dead are not where you have buried them, the debt is not what you have written in your ledgers. I have sat in rooms where my presence alone was treated as an accusation, and perhaps it was, perhaps the body of any man who has suffered is an accusation against the men who let him suffer, but I did not come to accuse. I came to bear witness, which is a stranger and a more dangerous thing, because the witness cannot lie and cannot leave, the witness must remain in the room until the truth has been spoken or the room has been emptied of everyone willing to hear it. And so I remain. I remain because I have nowhere else to stand and nothing else to give.

When I was a boy I believed that the world was waiting to receive me, that there was a place shaped exactly like my arrival, and it took me many years and much bitterness to understand that the place had been built for someone else and that I was expected to be grateful merely for the permission to stand near it. This is what a country does to its children when it has decided in advance which of them are real. It teaches them to apologize for the space their bodies take. It teaches them that hope is a kind of arrogance and that silence is a kind of safety, and both of these lessons are murders, slow and respectable murders, committed in good schools and clean churches by people who would faint to hear themselves called killers. I do not say this to wound. I say it because I have seen the children, I have seen what becomes of the brightness in their faces, and I cannot pretend that I did not see it. A man who has seen and will not say is worse than a man who was never given eyes. I was given eyes. I intend to use them, however it costs me, until they close.

There is a fire that does not consume but clarifies, and I have felt it, I have felt it rising in me in the worst of the long nights, when the news came and came and would not stop coming, when another name was added to the roll of those the country had decided it could spare. And I want to tell you that the danger is not the fire. The danger is the cold, the great national cold that calls itself reason, that calls itself law and order, that calls itself the way things have always been and must always be. I have been told to be calm by men who have never once in their lives had cause to be otherwise, and I have learned to hear in that word calm the sound of a door closing. They do not want my calm. They want my absence. They want a quiet so complete that they may mistake it for peace and sleep the untroubled sleep of those who have arranged the world to suit them. But I will not furnish that quiet. My voice is the small inheritance I was given, and I will spend it, and if it shakes the room a little, then let the room learn at last to hold a shaking thing.

I am often asked whether I have hope, as though hope were a possession one could display, and I have come to distrust the question, because I sense beneath it a longing to be excused. If I have hope, then perhaps the questioner need do nothing; my hope will carry the weight that his hands refuse. So I answer carefully. I say that hope is not a feeling but a decision, made again each morning, made in the teeth of every reason against it, and that no one can make my decision for me and I cannot make theirs. I have buried friends. I have watched the country I was born into deny, with a straight face and a clear conscience, the simplest facts of my existence and theirs. And still I rise, not because I am certain of victory, for I am certain of nothing, but because the alternative is to grant the lie the final word, and that I will not do, that I have sworn in the deepest part of myself never to do. We are responsible, all of us, for the world we hand to those who come after. I would not have them inherit my despair. Let them inherit, if nothing else, the proof that someone refused.
